The compact 9A-91 automatic carbine was developed in 1992 at the Tula Instrument Design Bureau as a more technologically advanced competitor to the SR-3 “Vikhr”. The 9A-91 operates using a gas-operated action with a rotating bolt featuring four locking lugs. The hammer-fired trigger mechanism allows for both semi-automatic and fully automatic fire. The safety-selector is located on the left side of the receiver above the trigger guard (on later versions it was moved to the right side, as a mounting rail for optical sights was added on the left). Early variants were equipped with a muzzle brake-compensator, which was later abandoned. The stock folds upward and forward and, like most of the weapon, is made of steel, with the exception of the polymer pistol grip and handguard. In the folded configuration, the weapon is suitable for concealed carry. For this purpose, the charging handle is also foldable. Unlike the Kalashnikov rifle, the charging handle slot remains permanently open.

AK-9

The AK-9 is a compact assault rifle developed by IzhMash based on the AK-74M, intended for special forces units of the Russian Armed Forces and Ministry of Internal Affairs. During development, designers aimed to outperform existing competitors such as the AS Val and SR-3M. The AK-9 is a shortened automatic weapon built on the standard AK-74M platform. Its main differences are a shortened barrel and gas system, as well as a redesigned pistol grip with significantly improved ergonomics. The rifle uses subsonic 9?39 mm cartridges such as SP-5, SP-6, and PAB-9. Unlike many other 9?39 mm weapons, the AK-9 does not suffer reliability issues when firing the more powerful and cheaper PAB-9 round. A quick-detach suppressor can be mounted on the barrel.

AKS-74U “Snag”

The AKS-74U was developed as a primary weapon for Spetsnaz, airborne troops, and special units, as well as for armored vehicle crews requiring a compact yet powerful automatic weapon. The AKS-74U is far more maneuverable in confined spaces and vehicles than the full-sized AKS-74. However, its short barrel and significantly reduced muzzle velocity result in a limited effective firing range. This particular rifle previously belonged to the stalker known as Snag.

ASVK

The ASVK (Army Large-Caliber Sniper Rifle; GRAU index 6V7 with optical and night sights) is a Russian large-caliber sniper rifle developed in 2004 by a design team at the Degtyaryov Plant in Kovrov, based on the KSVK and SVN-98 sniper rifle platforms. The ASVK is currently used exclusively by the Russian military. Some of these rifles have made their way into the Zone alongside several PMC units, suggesting possible ties between certain mercenary groups and the Russian government. It is relatively rare in the Zone and is typically used by mercenaries and duty patrols to eliminate dangerous mutants from a safe distance, as its powerful rounds are capable of killing almost any mutant.

The FAMAS G2 rifle, developed in 1994, differs from its predecessor, the FAMAS F1, primarily by its STANAG-compliant magazine well designed for M16 magazines, as well as a modified barrel rifling twist. It features the highest rate of fire among all rifles found in the Zone.

This futuristic-looking weapon is a mass-produced assault rifle manufactured by the Belgian company FN Herstal. Despite its bulky appearance, it offers excellent ergonomics, ease of handling in all firing modes, and high overall reliability.

FN FS2000 GL

This futuristic-looking weapon is a mass-produced assault rifle manufactured by FN Herstal. Despite its bulky appearance, it offers excellent ergonomics, handling, and reliability. The FS variant is equipped with the FN40GL underbarrel grenade launcher, derived from the GL1 launcher used in SCAR weapon systems and also compatible with the FN F/FS2000. It features a longer 443 mm barrel, which improves accuracy and increases muzzle energy.

FN F2000 “Tact”

This futuristic-looking weapon is a mass-produced assault rifle manufactured by FN Herstal. Despite its bulky appearance, it offers excellent ergonomics, handling, and reliability. This particular model has been heavily modified by Zone technicians, replacing the standard handguard with a tactical foregrip and adding a Picatinny rail mount for reflex sights. The weapon was clearly optimized for close-quarters combat, as evidenced by its increased rate of fire.

OTs-14-4A “Groza-4”

One of the variants of the OTs-14-4A weapon system. In the “Groza-4A” configuration, the rate of fire, trajectory flatness, and magazine capacity were improved through the use of the lighter 9?39 mm cartridge. This variant was produced only in small experimental batches. Some of these weapons made their way into the Zone but failed to gain widespread popularity due to unremarkable performance compared to other weapons of the same caliber. As a result, traders began replacing the standard 30-round magazine with a 60-round sector magazine and equipping the weapon with a Zenit “KLESH-2PS + LAM” LED flashlight, which slightly increased its popularity and demand.

One of the variants of the OTs-14-1A. In the “Groza-1” version, the rate of fire, trajectory flatness, and magazine capacity were improved through the use of the lighter 7.62x39 mm cartridge. This type of rifle was produced only in small experimental batches. Some of these weapons made their way into the Zone, but never gained much popularity due to unremarkable performance compared to other rifles of this caliber. As a result, traders simply replaced the standard 30-round magazine with a 60-round box magazine and equipped it with a Zenit “Kleshch-2PS + Laser” tactical flashlight, slightly increasing its popularity and demand.

OTs-14-2A “Groza”

OTs-14-2A is an experimental bullpup assault rifle variant of the Groza chambered in 5.45x39 mm. The project was never completed due to a preference for the more powerful 7.62x39 mm cartridge for this barrel length. In this case, the weapon represents a custom Zone-made conversion imitating the experimental variant through a careful barrel replacement, allowing it to fire the more common 5.45x39 mm cartridge. It has also been modified to use the more widespread PSO-1M optic.

KSVK 12.7

KSVK is a Russian .50 caliber (12.7x108 mm) anti-materiel rifle developed at the Degtyarev Plant in the late 1990s. It was designed to engage vehicles, counter-snipers, and enemies in heavy armor or behind dense cover. The KSVK is a bullpup rifle with manual operation and a rotating bolt (or straight-pull bolt, depending on the variant). It is considered moderately accurate, comparable to the American Barrett M82. Its strengths lie in extreme power and long effective range, though it is very heavy and cumbersome. Currently, the KSVK is used exclusively by Russian military forces. Some rifles have found their way into the Zone with PMC units, suggesting possible ties between certain mercenary groups and the Russian government. The rifle is rare in the Zone and typically used by mercenaries and guard units to eliminate dangerous mutants from a safe distance, as its powerful rounds can kill almost any mutant.

The shortened LR-300ML assault rifle represents a new step in the development of the legendary AR-15 family. Most changes affected only the upper receiver assembly, including the barrel, gas system, and bolt carrier group, resulting in improved ergonomics and reliability while reducing overall weight. This rifle offers high accuracy, although its high sensitivity to contamination makes it poorly suited for harsh Zone conditions.

The United States Navy Mark 14 Enhanced Battle Rifle (Mk 14 EBR) is an American designated marksman rifle developed by U.S. Navy Special Operations forces based on the M14 rifle. It is used by several U.S. Navy special units, including the SEALs.

 %c[d_purple] • %c[ui_gray_2] NATO suppressor

The PP-2000 is a Russian 9 mm submachine gun developed by a design team at the Tula Instrument Design Bureau under the leadership of V. P. Gryazev and A. G. Shipunov. The PP-2000 is intended for law enforcement units operating in urban environments, as well as a personal defense weapon for certain categories of military personnel. Serial production for the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs began in 2006. The weapon’s body is made of high-strength polymer. The barrel is chrome-lined and the weapon can be equipped with a suppressor, reflex sight, or optical sight. A universal mounting rail is installed on the receiver cover of production models.

CZ Scorpion EVO 3 A1

The Scorpion EVO 3 is a modern Czech submachine gun developed by ?esk? Zbrojovka in 2009. Its name references the older vz. 61 Skorpion (spelled with a “k”), though it is mechanically unrelated and belongs to a different class, being closer in design to weapons such as the MP5 or UMP. The Scorpion EVO is considered one of the best modern submachine guns. It is made from high-quality materials, very lightweight, compact, and comfortable to shoot, allowing long bursts with minimal recoil. Several countries have adopted the EVO for police, counter-terrorism, and special forces units, including the Czech Republic, Finland, Poland, Serbia, and Argentina. In the Zone, the EVO is mostly used by mercenaries and those who require a lightweight and compact weapon when carrying heavy loads or bulky primary weapons such as heavy sniper rifles, and need reliable close-range protection.

FN SCAR SSR Mk.20

The FN SCAR-SSR (Sniper Support Rifle) is the sniper variant of the 7.62 mm FN SCAR-H Mk.17 Mod.0 assault rifle used by U.S. special forces.

The SV-98 is a Russian bolt-action sniper rifle developed between 1998 and 2000 by a design team led by Vladimir Stronskiy and serially produced by the Izhmash concern. The SV-98 is designed to engage appearing, moving, exposed, and concealed enemy personnel, both unprotected and equipped with personal body armor, at distances of up to 1000 meters. The rifle is in service with and used by Ministry of Internal Affairs units.

SVD Ghillie

Originally intended for infantry marksmen within Soviet rifle squads, the SVD was not designed as a weapon for specialized sniper units. Relatively lightweight for a sniper rifle, well-balanced, and featuring semi-automatic fire, the SVD offers good but not exceptional accuracy. Its effective firing range reaches up to 800 meters. This variant is fitted with a ghillie camouflage covering, making user identification more difficult.

SVDK

The SVDK (GRAU Index 6V9) is a Russian large-caliber sniper rifle developed and adopted into service as part of the “Vzlomshchik” R&D program. It is based on the SVD platform and chambered for the powerful 9.3x64 mm 7N33 cartridge, a Russian military adaptation of the older 9.3x64 mm Brenneke hunting round. When fired from the SVDK, this round delivers muzzle energy of approximately 4,900 joules and is capable of penetrating up to 1 cm of armor with an 80% probability at a distance of 100 meters.

The TOchpribor OTs-03 SVU is a modernized version of the SVD sniper rifle, originally designed for the Soviet Airborne Forces but never mass-produced. In the early 1990s, the rifle was adopted by the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. Built in a compact bullpup configuration, the SVU is equipped with a powerful muzzle brake-compensator that reduces recoil and report.

SVU-AS “PMC”

A shortened sniper rifle with an increased rate of fire, representing the most compact variant of the SVU and SVD family. Its unique feature is a fully automatic firing mode, added at the request of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. Although this weapon is not intended for close combat, automatic fire can be useful in emergency situations when a sniper is detected by the enemy. The reduced size comes at the cost of lower accuracy and muzzle velocity. To compensate for heavy recoil during automatic fire, the SVU-AS is equipped with an integrated suppressor-flash hider, which also functions as an effective muzzle brake.

SVU “Sniper”

A unique custom-built variant of the SVU-AS “PMC”, rebuilt to a special order. The barrel was replaced with a full-length match-grade barrel featuring a 320 mm rifling twist. The trigger mechanism was completely reworked, with stamped trigger linkages replaced by tubular ones, significantly improving trigger feel, accuracy, and overall firing quality. These changes transformed the rifle into a truly precise, powerful sniper weapon. This particular rifle once belonged to Max, the legendary quartermaster of the Freedom faction.

Tigr-9

A modified Dragunov sniper rifle variant known as the SVD “Tigr”. Developed on the basis of the SVD and chambered for the powerful 9.3x64 mm 7N33 cartridge, the Russian military version of the older 9.3x64 mm Brenneke hunting round. It is very popular among hunters pursuing large game such as bears, moose, and wild boar. In the Zone, it is commonly encountered among artifact hunters and Clear Sky members.

A sniper rifle produced by the Finnish firearms manufacturer SAKO. The TRG-42 is not a modernization of an existing rifle, but a completely new design developed from scratch. Its consistently high accuracy and reliability have made it popular in shooting competitions and military operations requiring sniper support.

OTs-12 “Tiss”

The OTs-12 “Tiss” is a Russian assault rifle developed at the Tula Central Design Bureau of Sporting and Hunting Arms (TsKIB SOO) based on the AKS-74U. Its key difference is the use of special subsonic 9x39 mm cartridges (SP-5 and SP-6), which required changes to the barrel, muzzle device, bolt face dimensions, and magazine. The sights and muzzle brake-compensator were also modified. Production was planned at the Tula Arms Plant (TOZ), but never realized. The bullpup assault rifle “Groza”, developed a year later on the same basis, ultimately became far more popular.

TKPD Assault

The TKPD Assault carbine is a modified SVDK variant designed for assault operations and commissioned by the B.E.A.R. PMC, developed by SniperArms Dynamics. It is based on the SVD platform and chambered for the powerful 9.3x64 mm 7N33 cartridge, the Russian military adaptation of the Brenneke hunting round. A direct hit from a TKPD round almost guarantees the elimination of the target. It is used as a precise and powerful suppression weapon at medium ranges, with an effective firing distance of up to 800 meters.

TKPD-S

The TKPD-S carbine is a conversion variant of the TKPD, chambered in 7.62x54 mm 7N1. It is equipped with a modified trigger mechanism allowing automatic fire and uses extended 20-round magazines. The rifle features a reinforced match-grade barrel. Effective firing range is up to 800 meters.

The AS “Val” special assault rifle was developed on the basis of the VSS “Vintorez” suppressed sniper rifle. It was designed to equip special operations units of the Soviet Army and Ministry of Internal Affairs. Its primary role is the effective elimination of enemies equipped with modern personal armor without revealing the shooter’s position. Thanks to its integrated suppressor and the 9x39 mm cartridge with a heavy subsonic bullet, both firing sound and muzzle flash are reduced to a minimum.

AS “Val?MOD3”

The AS “Val” special assault rifle was developed on the basis of the VSS “Vintorez” suppressed sniper rifle. It was designed for arming special forces units of the Soviet Army and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The primary purpose of the rifle is the effective elimination of enemies using modern personal protection equipment without revealing the shooter’s position. Thanks to the integrated suppressor and the 9x39 mm cartridge with a heavy subsonic bullet, both the gunshot sound and muzzle flash are reduced to a minimum.

The SR?3 “Vikhr” is a compact Russian assault rifle developed in 1994 at TsNIITochMash in Klimovsk by designers A. D. Borisov and V. N. Levchenko. It was finalized for production by A. I. Tashlykov and entered serial production in 1996. It was created on the basis of the AS “Val” suppressed assault rifle and is unified with it in major components, which has a positive effect on production and operation. The SR?3’s design is generally similar to the AS “Val”: a gas?operated action and barrel locking via a bolt with six locking lugs. The SR?3M was developed later and features the ability to use a suppressor, metal 30?round magazines, mounting of optical and night sights, a left?folding skeletal stock (borrowed from the AS “Val”), an SVD?style safety selector, and a new handguard.

SR?3MT “Vikhr”

The Duty modification of the SR?3MT “Vikhr” is equipped with a tactical handguard manufactured in a custom batch specifically for Duty, which positively affected ergonomics and expanded equipment options.

PP?19 “Vityaz”

The PP?19?01 mod.10 is a Russian submachine gun developed in 2004 by Izhmash. Depending on the version, it is based on the AKS?74U (“Vityaz”) or the AK?105 (“Vityaz?SN”). It is a standard submachine gun used by personnel of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, police, Rosgvardiya, the Federal Penitentiary Service, and other law enforcement agencies. It represents a further development of the PP?19 “Bizon”. One of the main differences from the base PP?19?01 is the use of the AK?105 as the foundation instead of the AKS?74U. This is primarily expressed in the replacement of the receiver and fire control group with those of the AK?100 series, installation of the standard handguard and gas tube cover from the AK?74M family, as well as replacing the AKS?74U flip rear sight with an open sector sight.

The PP?19?01 mod.20 “Vityaz?SN” with a 30?round box magazine chambered in 9x19 mm was created in 2003 based on the design of the PP?19 “Bizon?2” submachine gun for the special purpose unit of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs “Vityaz”, commissioned by the Main Directorate of Scientific and Production Association “Special Equipment and Communications” of the MIA of Russia. It is mass?produced and supplied to various units of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs.
 One of the main differences of the “Vityaz?SN” from the base PP?19?01 is the use of the AK?105 as the foundation instead of the AKS?74U. This is primarily expressed in the replacement of the receiver and fire control group with those of the AK?100 series, installation of the standard handguard and gas tube cover from the AK?74M family, as well as replacing the AKS?74U flip rear sight with an open sector sight.

The M16 (official designation: Rifle, Caliber 5.56 mm, M16) is an American automatic rifle chambered in 5.56?45 mm, developed from the AR?15 and adopted in the 1960s. In 1964, the M16 officially entered service, replacing the M14, and by 1966 it was issued to all U.S. units in Vietnam. Early versions proved to be extremely unreliable. However, by the early 1970s the M16 had matured into a fully capable combat weapon with a number of significant advantages (and, of course, some drawbacks). Compared to its main global rival, the Kalashnikov AKM, the M16 offered greater accuracy and tighter shot grouping in semi?automatic fire and was generally more comfortable to handle. On the other hand, it required more careful maintenance and higher?quality ammunition. In particularly harsh conditions such as dirt and dust, the AKM surpassed the M16 in reliability. The M16 and its variants remain in service with U.S. infantry to this day and are among the most widespread small arms in the world, with over 8 million units produced.

The hammer?type fire control mechanism allows both semi?automatic and fully automatic fire. The fire selector is combined with the safety and can be confidently operated even while wearing gloves. Cyclic rate ranges from 800 to 1000 rounds per minute. Effective accuracy is maintained up to 50 meters, with a maximum effective range of approximately 100 meters.
